overview.intro:
Chapter 06 covers what nurseries and florists sell: dormant and growing bulbs, live plants, cuttings and mushroom spawn, cut flowers, and foliage and branches, including fresh-cut Christmas trees. Its **78 tariff lines** carry low rates: a few cents per 1,000 bulbs, 1.4% to 4.8% on plants, **6.8% on fresh roses** and **6.4% on most other cut flowers**, and Free on fresh foliage, fruit trees, rose plants and orchid plants.

The U.S. imported **$4.05B** of these goods in 2025; cut flowers were 67% of it, and Colombia and Ecuador supplied 85% of the cut flowers. Since **July 24, 2026** a **Section 301 tariff** applies on top: **12.5% on Colombian flowers** even with an FTA claim, 10% in total on EU goods, 10% or 12.5% for most other suppliers — but **Ecuador's exception list** keeps almost all Ecuadorian flowers at their base rate. Since **August 22, 2026** Canadian bulbs, cuttings, orchids and cut flowers pay a **50% Section 338 duty**, USMCA claim or not. Every plant also needs USDA APHIS clearance.

productGroups.label: Bulbs, tubers & corms
productGroups.blurb: Dormant tulip, hyacinth, lily, narcissus and crocus bulbs and lily-of-the-valley pips pay a few cents to $1.44 per 1,000 (well under 1% of value); other dormant bulbs 3.5%, bulbs in growth 1.4%. The Netherlands supplied 72% of 2025 imports, and EU bulbs now pay 10% of value in total.

productGroups.label: Live plants, cuttings & nursery stock
productGroups.blurb: Free on fruit and nut trees, rose plants and orchid plants; 1.4% to 4.8% on cuttings, perennials, azaleas, poinsettias and other trees and shrubs; 1.4¢/kg on mushroom spawn. Unrooted cuttings (0602.10) are the only Chapter 06 line exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Cut flowers
productGroups.blurb: Fresh roses pay 6.8%, miniature carnations 3.2%, other fresh cut flowers 6.4% and dried or dyed flowers 4%; FTA partners and AGOA countries pay no base rate. Colombian flowers pay a 12.5% Section 301 duty; Ecuadorian flowers are on Ecuador's exception list.

productGroups.label: Foliage, branches & Christmas trees
productGroups.blurb: Free on all fresh foliage — including fresh-cut Christmas trees, ferns, eucalyptus and palms — and on mosses and dried foliage; 7% on other foliage that is dyed or otherwise prepared.

workedExamples.title: $50,000 of fresh roses from Colombia
workedExamples.body: Roses carry a 6.8% base rate, which the Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement (SPI **CO**) makes Free. The 12.5% Section 301 duty on goods of Colombia (9903.05.32) still applies with the FTA claim (U.S. note 52(a)): **$6,250**. Without the CO claim the shipment would pay 6.8% + 12.5% = 19.3%, or **$9,650**.

workedExamples.title: The same roses from Ecuador
workedExamples.body: There is no FTA with Ecuador and GSP has been expired since 2020, so the **6.8%** base rate applies: **$3,400**. Roses are on Ecuador's exception list (U.S. note 52(j)(12), heading 9903.06.18), so the 10% Section 301 duty on Ecuador (9903.05.35) does not apply. That is why Ecuadorian roses now pay less than Colombian ones with an FTA claim.

workedExamples.title: 100,000 tulip bulbs from the Netherlands
workedExamples.body: The base rate is 89.6¢ per 1,000 bulbs: **$89.60**. For EU goods the 2026 Section 301 rule (9903.05.39) sets the total at 10% of value when the base rate is lower, so a $15,000 shipment pays **$1,500** in total. Bulbs are plants for planting: they also need an APHIS permit and a Dutch phytosanitary certificate.

workedExamples.title: Cut tulips and nursery stock from Canada
workedExamples.body: Canadian cut flowers other than carnations are on the Section 338 list (9903.03.14): $20,000 of USMCA-qualifying cut tulips pays **$10,000** (50%). Without USMCA it is 6.4% + 10% + 50% = 66.4%, or $13,280. By contrast, USMCA-qualifying Canadian trees, shrubs and poinsettias (0602.90.60) and Christmas trees (0604.20) are not on the list and enter **free**.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 06: Live Trees and Other Plants; Bulbs, Roots and the Like; Cut Flowers and Ornamental Foliage — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 06 Tariff Updates 2026: Flowers from Colombia & Ecuador, Canadian Plants, Section 301 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for live plants, bulbs and cut flowers since January 2025: unchanged base rates, the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (12.5% on Colombian flowers, Ecuador's exception list), Canada's 50% Section 338 duty and APHIS's chrysanthemum rule, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 06 base rate changed: all 78 lines read the same.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties (the reciprocal tariff on every supplier, and +25% or +35% on Mexican and Canadian goods that did not qualify for USMCA) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** plants and flowers from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**: **12.5% on Colombian flowers** even with an FTA claim, 10% in total on Dutch bulbs. **Ecuador's exception list** keeps almost all Ecuadorian flowers at their base rate, and Guatemala and Taiwan have similar lists. Since **August 22, 2026** a **50% Section 338 duty** applies to 48 lines from **Canada** — bulbs, cuttings, orchids and cut flowers — even with a USMCA claim. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers these goods.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 06 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies with their exemption and country exception lists, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, China's Section 301 List 4A, the Canada Section 338 duty, the scheduled Nicaragua tariff, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, and APHIS rule changes for plants and cut flowers. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: +12.5% on 77 of 78 lines (9903.05.32); Unrooted cuttings and slips (0602.10) are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). The Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement (CO) makes the base rate Free but does not remove the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)), and Colombia has no country exception list. The IEEPA reciprocal duty ended February 24, 2026, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge expired July 23, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Fresh roses from Colombia claimed under CO pay 12.5% of value — $6,250 on a $50,000 shipment. Without the claim they pay 6.8% + 12.5% = 19.3%. Colombia supplied $1.61B of U.S. cut-flower imports in 2025.

inEffect.now: +50% on 48 lines (USMCA or not); +10% more without USMCA
inEffect.exemption: Two duties. The Section 338 duty (9903.03.14) adds 50% from August 22, 2026 on 48 of 78 lines — bulbs, unrooted cuttings, orchid plants, mushroom spawn, fresh cut flowers other than carnations, dried flowers and non-fresh foliage — with or without a USMCA claim (U.S. note 51(a)). The 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.29) adds 10% on 77 lines but not on USMCA-qualifying goods (9903.05.93). Nursery stock, carnations and fresh foliage, including Christmas trees, are not on the Section 338 list. The 2025 IEEPA duty (+35% on non-USMCA goods) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: USMCA-qualifying Canadian nursery stock and Christmas trees enter free, but USMCA-qualifying Canadian cut tulips or potted orchids pay 50% of value. Canadian cut flowers that do not qualify pay 6.4% + 10% + 50% = 66.4%.

inEffect.now: +10% on 8 lines; exception list on the rest
inEffect.exemption: Ecuador's exception list (U.S. note 52(j)(12), 9903.06.18) covers 69 of the 78 lines, including every fresh cut flower, dried flowers, foliage, dormant tulip, lily and narcissus bulbs and rooted plants with soil. Unrooted cuttings and slips (0602.10) are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). The 10% duty (9903.05.35) applies only to 8 lines: lily-of-the-valley pips, hyacinth bulbs in growth, fruit and nut trees, rhododendrons and azaleas, herbaceous perennials and other plants without soil, and mushroom spawn. There is no FTA with Ecuador and GSP has been expired since December 31, 2020, so the base rate applies. The IEEPA reciprocal duty ended February 24, 2026, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge expired July 23, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Ecuadorian roses pay only the 6.8% base rate — $3,400 on a $50,000 shipment — and other cut flowers 6.4%.

inEffect.whatItMeans: Brazilian plants and flowers pay the base rate plus 37.5% of value; unrooted cuttings pay 4.8% + 25% = 29.8%.

Country exception lists in U.S. note 52(j) remove the duty on most Chapter 06 lines for Switzerland, Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia and Jordan, and on a few lines for El Salvador, Argentina and Bangladesh. changes.title: No Chapter 06 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 78 Chapter 06 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered.

changes.title: APHIS lifts chrysanthemum white rust restrictions on cut flowers and cuttings (from November 9, 2026)
changes.detail: A final rule removes every chrysanthemum white rust (CWR) condition on fresh cut chrysanthemums (genera Chrysanthemum, Leucanthemella and Nipponanthemum) and moves the commodity-specific cut-flower conditions out of 7 CFR 319.74 into APHIS's Agricultural Commodity Import Requirements (ACIR) database, effective November 9, 2026. A companion notice deregulates CWR as a quarantine pest and allows Chrysanthemum cuttings and in vitro plantlets to be authorized from certain countries from the same date. No duty changes: cut chrysanthemums (0603.14) stay at 6.4% and unrooted cuttings (0602.10) at 4.8%.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 list rewritten; Chapter 06 lines unchanged
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 added and removed products on the Section 338 list for goods of Canada (9903.03.14) from September 15, 2026 and made the duty apply on top of Section 232 duties. None of the 48 Chapter 06 lines on the list was added or removed; they have paid the 50% since August 22, 2026.

changes.title: Section 338 duty of 50% on Canadian bulbs, cuttings and cut flowers
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 (motor vehicles) put a 50% duty on listed products of Canada (9903.03.14), first from August 19, then, after Proclamation 11056 suspended it for three days, from August 22, 2026. The list includes 48 of the 78 Chapter 06 lines: tulip, hyacinth, lily and narcissus bulbs, other dormant bulbs (0601.10.90), hyacinths in growth, unrooted cuttings, orchid plants, mushroom spawn, all fresh cut flowers except carnations, dried flowers, and mosses, dried and other non-fresh foliage. It applies even with a USMCA claim (U.S. note 51(a)). Nursery stock (trees, shrubs, perennials, poinsettias, rose plants), carnations and all fresh foliage, including Christmas trees, are not listed.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover almost every bulb, plant and flower
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) from July 24, 2026, on 77 of the 78 Chapter 06 lines; only unrooted cuttings and slips (0602.10) are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). Colombia, Costa Rica, Peru and Thailand pay 12.5%; Ecuador, Guatemala, India, Mexico and Canada 10%; EU goods 10% in total and Taiwan 10% in total. Country exception lists remove it for most cut flowers from Ecuador (69 lines), Guatemala (55) and Taiwan (56). USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94); other FTA claims do not remove it (U.S. note 52(a)).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. The next day the 2026 Section 301 tariffs took over for 60 economies.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all products of Brazil (9903.05.01) from July 22, 2026; the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)) has no Chapter 06 line. Two days later Brazil also became subject to the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.27), so Brazilian plants and flowers pay the base rate plus 37.5% (25% on unrooted cuttings).

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian and Mexican plants and flowers. They do not remove the Canada Section 338 duty.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Its product exemption list (9903.03.03) had no Chapter 06 subheading, so bulbs, plants and flowers paid it from every supplier; USMCA goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. No Chapter 06 line had been on the reciprocal tariff's agricultural exemption list (9903.01.32), so flowers from Colombia, for example, had paid the 10% baseline since April 2025. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: Legislation signed February 3, 2026 renewed AGOA through December 31, 2026, retroactive to September 30, 2025, when it had lapsed. AGOA (SPI D) makes every dutiable Chapter 06 line Free for listed sub-Saharan countries such as Kenya, which is not one of the 60 Section 301 economies, so Kenyan roses and cuttings enter duty-free. GSP (SPI A, A*, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua scheduled: 10% in 2027, 15% in 2028
changes.detail: USTR's Nicaragua action phases in a tariff on Nicaraguan goods that do not originate under CAFTA-DR (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028. It reaches all 78 Chapter 06 lines. Nicaragua is also one of the 60 economies paying the 2026 Section 301 duty; CAFTA-DR claims do not remove that one (U.S. note 52(a)).

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: APHIS authorizes potted Phalaenopsis orchids from Germany and the Netherlands
changes.detail: Phalaenopsis orchid plants for planting may be imported from Germany and the Netherlands established in approved growing media, under the Plants for Planting Manual and a bilateral workplan, instead of bare-root only. Duty: orchid plants (0602.90.20) have a Free base rate, so EU orchids pay the 10% Section 301 duty since July 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and higher country rates (9903.02.xx) on every Chapter 06 line; Canada and Mexico were excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing duty orders on cut flowers revoked in 1999
changes.detail: Commerce revoked the orders on fresh cut flowers from Colombia, standard chrysanthemums from the Netherlands and standard carnations from Kenya in May 1999, and the USITC terminated their five-year reviews. We found no antidumping or countervailing duty order in force on any Chapter 06 product; check CBP's AD/CVD case search before entry.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 06 goods grew from **$2.56B in 2020 to $4.16B in 2024**, then slipped to **$4.05B in 2025** (-2.6%). Cut flowers held steady at $2.73B ($2.70B in 2024): **Colombia** ($1.61B) and **Ecuador** ($706M) supply 85% of them, and fresh roses alone were $1.25B, 31% of the chapter. The fall came from live plants ($981M to $878M) and foliage ($263M to $218M): **Canada**, whose exports are mostly live plants ($538M), fell 7.4%, and **China** fell 32%. The **Netherlands** grew 10.5% to $305M and supplied 72% of the bulbs.

Base rates did not change. In 2025 most suppliers paid the IEEPA reciprocal tariff from April (10% for Colombia, for example), and Canadian and Mexican goods that did not qualify for USMCA paid 25% or 35%; those duties ended February 24, 2026. The 2026 Section 301 and Section 338 duties started in July and August 2026 and are not yet in a full year of trade data. These are values, not volumes. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on plants and flowers depends more on **where they come from** than on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

**Colombian flowers pay 12.5%** with a Colombia TPA claim; **Ecuadorian flowers pay only their 6.4% to 6.8% base rate** because Ecuador's exception list removes the Section 301 duty. **Dutch bulbs and flowers pay 10% in total.** USMCA-qualifying Mexican goods are free, but **Canada's bulbs, cuttings, orchids and cut flowers pay 50%** under Section 338 even with USMCA, while its nursery stock and Christmas trees enter free. Costa Rica, Peru and Thailand pay 12.5%; Kenya, under AGOA, pays nothing.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 06: Live Trees and Other Plants; Bulbs, Roots and the Like; Cut Flowers and Ornamental Foliage — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Plants & Cut Flowers into the U.S.: APHIS Permits, CITES & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 06) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The USDA APHIS, CITES and CBP rules for each HTS Chapter 06 line — plants-for-planting permits and phytosanitary certificates, cut-flower inspection, Christmas trees from Canada, CITES orchids, origin marking — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTA and AGOA claims, the unrooted-cuttings exemption and country exception lists.
keywords: usda aphis plant propagation import regulations

tariffEngineering.intro:
Before a plant or flower shipment pays any duty it has to be **allowed in**. Bulbs, cuttings and nursery stock are "plants for planting": they need a written APHIS permit unless the Plants for Planting Manual exempts them, a phytosanitary certificate, usually entry through a USDA plant inspection station, and no soil. Cut flowers are inspected at the port of first arrival. Orchids, cacti and other CITES-listed plants need CITES documents, and Christmas trees from Canada may need a certificate.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA**, an **FTA** or **AGOA**, ship cuttings **unrooted** (the only Chapter 06 line exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty), and check whether the line is on the supplier's **country exception list**. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation. None of them removes Canada's 50% Section 338 duty.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on plants and flowers from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 7%) and the 10% Section 301 duty on goods of Canada or Mexico
levers.appliesTo: All 78 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA — plants grown in Canada or Mexico qualify
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. No prescribed form; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on the 48 listed lines from Canada (U.S. note 51(a)): Canadian bulbs, unrooted cuttings, orchid plants, mushroom spawn and cut flowers other than carnations pay it either way. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim the FTA rate (Colombia, CAFTA-DR, Peru, Chile, Israel and others)
levers.saves: The base rate — 6.8% on roses, 6.4% on most cut flowers, up to 4.8% on plants
levers.appliesTo: The 59 dutiable lines, which are Free for FTA partners (SPI AU, BH, CL, CO, IL, JO, KR, MA, OM, P, PA, PE, SG), for CBERA countries (E) and, on some lines, for Japan (JP)
levers.document: The claim and certification each agreement requires — for example 19 CFR 10.3003 (Colombia) or 19 CFR 10.583 (CAFTA-DR).
levers.caveat: An FTA claim removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty for the country (U.S. note 52(a)): Colombian roses claimed under CO still pay 12.5%. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Source from an AGOA country outside the Section 301 list (Kenya and others)
levers.saves: Everything: the base rate is Free under AGOA (D), and Kenya is not one of the 60 Section 301 economies
levers.appliesTo: The 59 dutiable lines (all carry D in the Special column), for goods of the countries listed in General Note 16
levers.document: An AGOA claim (SPI D) on the entry, for goods that meet the origin rules of General Note 16 (plants grown in the beneficiary country qualify).
levers.caveat: AGOA is authorized only through December 31, 2026. Some AGOA countries (for example South Africa, Nigeria and Angola) are among the 60 Section 301 economies and still pay that duty.

citations.label: USTR statement on the AGOA reauthorization (February 3, 2026)

levers.title: Ship cuttings unrooted
levers.saves: The whole 2026 Section 301 duty — 10% or 12.5% of value — on cuttings and slips
levers.appliesTo: Unrooted cuttings and slips (0602.10.00), the only Chapter 06 line on the general exemption list; rooted cuttings and young plants classify in 0602.90 and pay it
levers.document: Correct classification on the entry (0602.10.00), backed by the plants-for-planting permit and phytosanitary certificate describing unrooted cuttings.
levers.caveat: The exemption (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86) removes only the 2026 Section 301 duty. Chinese cuttings still pay 7.5% (List 4A), Brazilian ones 25%, and Canadian unrooted cuttings are on the Section 338 list (50%).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(b)

levers.title: Check the supplier country's exception list
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty on most lines from Ecuador, Guatemala and Taiwan (and Switzerland, Indonesia, Cambodia, Jordan, Malaysia)
levers.appliesTo: Lines on the country lists in U.S. note 52(j) — for Ecuador every fresh cut flower and 69 of 78 lines; for Guatemala 55 lines; for Taiwan orchid plants, cut flowers and foliage (56 lines)
levers.document: Correct classification and country of origin on the entry; the exception heading (for example 9903.06.18 for Ecuador) is reported with it.
levers.caveat: The lists are per country and per line: Ecuadorian mushroom spawn and plants without soil, and Guatemalan dormant bulbs and chrysanthemums, still pay 10%. The lists can change with each Agreement on Reciprocal Trade.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(j)

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (dormant vs. in growth, with vs. without soil, rooted vs. unrooted, bouquet with accessories) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate, the exemption-list status or the Section 338 status
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the goods.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own.

rules.title: Plants for planting (bulbs, cuttings, nursery stock): written PPQ permit unless the Plants for Planting Manual exempts the plant (apply at least 30 days before arrival), phytosanitary certificate naming the genus, entry through a USDA plant inspection station unless precleared, free of soil except from Canada or in approved growing media; some taxa are not authorized pending pest risk analysis or need postentry quarantine

Fresh cut flowers: held at the port of first arrival for APHIS inspection; treatment (e.g. methyl bromide for leafminers) if pests are found. Chrysanthemum white rust restrictions end November 9, 2026, when commodity conditions move to ACIR
Commodity- and country-specific entry conditions (greenery, foliage, dried plant material, mushroom spawn and cut flowers) are listed in the Agricultural Commodity Import Requirements (ACIR) database

citations.label: 7 CFR 319.74-1 (what counts as a cut flower)

rules.title: Christmas trees from Canada: trees without roots going to or through U.S. areas free of gypsy (spongy) moth need a phytosanitary certificate (from infested areas of Canada) or a certificate of origin (from non-infested areas), unless greenhouse-grown

CITES-listed plants (most orchids, cacti, cycads, some bulbs such as snowdrops and cyclamen): CITES export or re-export document, entry through a designated port, and an APHIS protected-plant permit for businesses; cut flowers of artificially propagated Appendix II plants are usually excluded by the listing annotation

Country-of-origin marking: cut flowers, plants and nursery stock, and Christmas trees are on the J-list, so the article itself need not be marked, but the outermost container must show the country of origin

groups.label: Bulbs, tubers & corms
groups.note: Bulbs are plants for planting even when dormant. Some bulbous plants (for example Galanthus snowdrops and Cyclamen) are CITES-listed. Canadian tulip, hyacinth, lily and narcissus bulbs pay the 50% Section 338 duty.

groups.label: Live plants, cuttings & nursery stock
groups.note: Most orchids and cacti are CITES-listed. Potted Phalaenopsis orchids from Germany and the Netherlands may enter in approved growing media (since July 22, 2025); chrysanthemum cuttings from certain countries may be authorized from November 9, 2026. Mushroom spawn is not a plant for planting; check ACIR.

groups.label: Cut flowers
groups.note: Bouquets and wreaths classify with the flowers they are made of (chapter note 2). Dried, dyed or bleached flowers (0603.90) are not "cut flowers" under 7 CFR 319.74-1; their conditions are in ACIR.

groups.label: Foliage, branches & Christmas trees
groups.note: Fresh greenery and Christmas trees are not "cut flowers" under 7 CFR 319.74-1; Christmas trees from Canada fall under the gypsy (spongy) moth rules. Fresh foliage and Christmas trees are not on Canada's Section 338 list.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing flowers, plants and bulbs into the U.S. — tariffs by country, HS codes and entry rules. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Base rates are low and unchanged: 6.8% on fresh roses, 6.4% on most cut flowers, 1.4% to 4.8% on plants, Free on fresh foliage and Christmas trees. The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026.

Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff applies to 60 economies: 12.5% on Colombian flowers even with the FTA, 10% in total on EU bulbs and flowers — but Ecuador's exception list keeps nearly all Ecuadorian flowers at their base rate.
Canadian bulbs, cuttings, orchids and cut flowers have paid a 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026, even with USMCA; Canadian nursery stock and Christmas trees still enter free under USMCA.
Unrooted cuttings are the only Chapter 06 line exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, and Kenyan flowers enter free under AGOA.
Every bulb and plant needs APHIS clearance (permit, phytosanitary certificate, no soil), cut flowers are inspected at the port, and CITES-listed orchids and cacti need CITES documents.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on flowers imported into the U.S.?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on flowers
tariffs on flowers from south america
faqs.answer: Yes. Fresh cut flowers carry a base rate of 3.2% to 6.8% (roses 6.8%, most others 6.4%) and dried or dyed flowers 4%. FTA partners such as Colombia, Peru, Chile and the CAFTA-DR countries pay no base rate, and Kenya pays nothing under AGOA. Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff applies on top to flowers from 60 economies: 12.5% for Colombia, Costa Rica and Peru, and 10% in total for the EU. Ecuador's exception list removes it for every Ecuadorian cut flower. Canadian cut flowers other than carnations pay a 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026, even with USMCA. The IEEPA tariffs of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on flowers from Colombia?
searchedAs: tariffs on flowers from south america
faqs.answer: 12.5% of value with a Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement (CO) claim: the FTA makes the base rate Free, but the 2026 Section 301 duty on goods of Colombia (9903.05.32, since July 24, 2026) still applies. Without the claim roses pay 6.8% + 12.5% = 19.3% and other cut flowers 18.9%. Colombia has no exception list. The 10% IEEPA reciprocal tariff of 2025 ended February 24, 2026, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ran from then until July 23, 2026. Colombia supplied $1.66B (41%) of U.S. imports of plants and flowers in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on flowers from Ecuador?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on flowers from ecuador
faqs.answer: Only the base rate on cut flowers: 6.8% on roses and 6.4% on most others. Ecuador's exception list (9903.06.18) removes the 10% Section 301 duty on 69 of the 78 Chapter 06 lines, including every fresh cut flower. The 10% still applies to 8 lines, such as lily-of-the-valley pips, fruit trees, plants without soil and mushroom spawn. There is no FTA with Ecuador and GSP has been expired since 2020. Ecuador supplied $722M of plants and flowers in 2025, almost all cut flowers.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on roses, and what is their HS code?
searchedAs: hs code for fresh cut roses
faqs.answer: Fresh cut roses are 0603.11.00 (statistical suffix 30 for spray roses, 50 for others), with a 6.8% base rate that FTA partners and AGOA countries do not pay. Live rose plants, grafted or not, are 0602.40.00, Free. What you pay depends on the country: Colombian roses 12.5% with the FTA, Ecuadorian roses 6.8%, Dutch roses 10%, USMCA-qualifying Canadian cut roses 50% (Section 338), Kenyan roses Free. Fresh roses were the largest Chapter 06 import in 2025 at $1.25B.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on plants from Canada?
faqs.answer: It depends on the plant. Canadian nursery stock — trees and shrubs, perennials, poinsettias, azaleas, rose and fruit plants — enters free with a USMCA claim. But 48 of the 78 Chapter 06 lines, including bulbs, unrooted cuttings, orchid plants, mushroom spawn and cut flowers other than carnations, pay a 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14) since August 22, 2026, with or without USMCA. Goods that do not qualify for USMCA also pay the base rate plus 10% Section 301. The 35% IEEPA duty ended February 24, 2026. Canada supplied $767M in 2025, $538M of it live plants.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on Christmas trees from Canada?
searchedAs: tariffs on christmas trees from canada
are there tariffs on christmas trees
are there tariffs on christmas trees from canada
faqs.answer: Not on USMCA-qualifying fresh-cut trees. Christmas trees (0604.20.00.20 Douglas fir, .40 other fir, .60 other) have a Free base rate and are not on Canada's Section 338 list, so trees that qualify for USMCA pay nothing; trees that do not qualify pay 10% under Section 301 (9903.05.29). Trees going to U.S. areas free of gypsy (spongy) moth need a Canadian phytosanitary certificate or certificate of origin (7 CFR 319.77-4). Artificial Christmas trees are a different product (9505.10.40.10 or 9505.10.50.10).

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on flower bulbs from the Netherlands?
faqs.answer: Yes, 10% of value in total since July 24, 2026. Dormant bulbs (0601.10) have tiny per-1,000 base rates — tulips 89.6¢, hyacinths 38.4¢, lilies 55.7¢, narcissus $1.34, crocus 19.2¢ — and other bulbs 3.5%. For EU goods the 2026 Section 301 rule (9903.05.39) sets the total at 10% when the base rate is lower, which it is on every bulb line. The Netherlands supplied $159M (72%) of U.S. bulb imports in 2025. Bulbs also need an APHIS permit and a phytosanitary certificate.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for fresh cut flowers?
searchedAs: hs code for fresh cut flowers
faqs.answer: Heading 0603. Fresh: 0603.11 roses (6.8%), 0603.12 carnations (3.2% miniature spray, 6.4% other), 0603.13 orchids, 0603.14 chrysanthemums, 0603.15 lilies and 0603.19.01 other fresh flowers (all 6.4%), with 10-digit lines for alstroemeria, gerbera, hydrangea, sunflowers, tulips and others. 0603.90 covers dried, dyed, bleached or otherwise prepared flowers (4%). Bouquets and wreaths classify with the flowers they are made of (chapter note 2).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for dried and artificial flowers?
faqs.answer: Dried, dyed or bleached flowers are 0603.90.00 (4%); dried or bleached foliage is 0604.90.30 (Free) and other prepared foliage 0604.90.60 (7%). Artificial flowers are not in Chapter 06: they are heading 6702 — plastic flowers 6702.10.20 (8.4%, assembled by binding) or 6702.10.40 (3.4%), and flowers of other materials 6702.90 (feathers 4.7%, man-made fibers 9%, other 17%).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for live plants?
faqs.answer: Heading 0602 (bulbs are 0601): unrooted cuttings 0602.10 (4.8%), fruit and nut trees 0602.20 (Free), rhododendrons and azaleas 0602.30 (1.9%), rose plants 0602.40 (Free), orchid plants 0602.90.20 (Free), other herbaceous perennials 0602.90.30 with soil (1.4%) or 0602.90.40 without (3.5%), mushroom spawn 0602.90.50 (1.4¢/kg), and other plants, trees, shrubs and poinsettias 0602.90.60 with soil (1.9%) or 0602.90.90 without (4.8%). The U.S. imported $878M of live plants in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for mushroom spawn?
faqs.answer: 0602.90.50.00, at 1.4¢/kg (Column 2: 2.2¢/kg) and Free for FTA partners and AGOA countries. It is the one Chapter 06 line not on China's List 4A, so Chinese spawn pays the base rate plus the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty; Canadian spawn pays the 50% Section 338 duty. Fresh mushrooms themselves are vegetables in Chapter 07 (heading 0709).

faqs.question: How do I import live plants into the U.S.? Do I need an APHIS permit?
searchedAs: can you import plants into the us
bringing plants into us from canada
faqs.answer: Usually yes. Plants for planting — bulbs, cuttings, nursery stock — need a written APHIS PPQ permit unless the Plants for Planting Manual exempts them (7 CFR 319.37-5); apply at least 30 days before arrival. Each shipment needs a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country (319.37-6), permit shipments must enter through a USDA plant inspection station unless precleared (319.37-8), and plants must be free of soil except from Canada or in approved growing media (319.37-10). Some taxa are not authorized pending pest risk analysis (319.37-4). CITES-listed plants such as most orchids and cacti also need CITES documents.

faqs.question: Can you bring tulip bulbs into the U.S.?
searchedAs: can you bring tulip bulbs into the us
faqs.answer: Yes, but bulbs are plants for planting, so APHIS rules apply: a written permit unless the Plants for Planting Manual exempts them (permit-exempt plants still need an inspector's oral authorization at the port, 7 CFR 319.37-5(e)), a phytosanitary certificate, no soil, and inspection on arrival. Commercial shipments also pay duty: tulip bulbs (0601.10.15) carry 89.6¢ per 1,000, and Dutch bulbs pay 10% of value in total under the 2026 Section 301 rule for EU goods.
